scenes.text: Here's the thigh muscle we finished on, working hard, with a supply line running back to the chest. Run up a flight of stairs and two things happen at once: you breathe harder, and your heart beats faster. They're different systems, with different organs. So why do both change together? And how does oxygen actually get from the air into that muscle?

Air takes a fixed route. Through the nose, it's warmed, moistened and filtered. It passes the pharynx and the larynx, then the trachea, held open by rings of cartilage. The trachea splits into two bronchi, one to each lung, which branch into narrower bronchioles. They end in the alveoli, hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, and that's where all gas exchange happens. Everything before them is plumbing. Alveoli are built for exchange: a huge surface, walls one cell thick, a dense net of capillaries, and a difference in oxygen that stays steep, because breathing and blood flow keep refreshing it.

Air isn't sucked in. It flows in when the chest gets bigger. Breathing in is always active. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals lift the ribs up and out. The chest's volume rises, its pressure falls below the air outside, and air flows in. Quiet breathing out is passive. Those muscles relax, the lungs recoil, and air flows out. In hard exercise, breathing out becomes active too, as the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals squeeze the air out faster.

Now the pump. The heart has four chambers, split down the middle by a wall called the septum, so the two sides never mix. The upper chambers, the atria, receive blood. The lower chambers, the ventricles, pump it out. The right side sends blood to the lungs. The left side sends it to the whole body, which is why the left ventricle has the thickest wall. Four valves keep the flow one way: the tricuspid on the right, the bicuspid on the left, and a semilunar valve where blood leaves each ventricle.

The vessels match their jobs. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, under high pressure, so their walls are thick, muscular and elastic. Smaller arterioles act as taps. In exercise, they open towards working muscle and close down elsewhere. Capillaries have walls one cell thick, and they're the only place exchange happens. Veins return blood at low pressure, with one-way valves, and contracting muscles squeeze them, pumping blood back up. The blood itself is mostly plasma, carrying red cells with haemoglobin for oxygen, white cells for defence, and platelets for clotting.

So follow the blood. The heart runs two circuits, one after the other. In the pulmonary circulation, blood from the body enters the right atrium through the vena cava, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped out through the pulmonary valve, along the pulmonary artery to the lungs. It picks up oxygen and returns through the pulmonary vein to the left atrium. In the systemic circulation, it passes the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, and out through the aortic valve into the aorta, to the body's capillaries, then back through the veins to the vena cava.

Now the mark most often lost. Arteries aren't defined by carrying oxygenated blood. They're defined by carrying blood away from the heart. In the body, that blood happens to be rich in oxygen. But the pulmonary artery carries blood low in oxygen to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood back. Learn the direction rule, and the exception stops being an exception.

Gas exchange is diffusion: gases move from where their partial pressure is higher to where it's lower, and no energy is spent moving them. Partial pressure is the share of the pressure one gas contributes. At the alveoli, oxygen is at about a hundred and four, and the arriving blood is at about forty, so oxygen moves into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves out. At the working muscle, it reverses. The blood arrives at about a hundred. The muscle's is about forty, lower in exercise, because it's using oxygen up. So oxygen moves in, and carbon dioxide moves into the blood. In between, about ninety-eight per cent of the oxygen rides on haemoglobin.

So why do breathing and heart rate rise together? Both answer the same signals. The brain's respiratory centre sets breathing, and it responds mainly to rising carbon dioxide, detected by chemical sensors called chemoreceptors. Sensors in muscles and joints detect movement too. Carbon dioxide, not low oxygen, is the main trigger. And exchange speeds up in exercise for three reasons. The working muscle steepens the gradients. More capillaries open. And haemoglobin lets go of oxygen more easily where it's warm and acidic, which is exactly the muscle that needs it.
Two things to remember. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen. And gas exchange is diffusion, twice, always down the gradient.
Two exam questions. First. Explain how carbon dioxide produced in a working muscle cell reaches the air you breathe out. Pause here to answer.

Carbon dioxide diffuses from the muscle, where its partial pressure is higher, into the blood. Veins carry it to the right atrium, and the right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. There, it diffuses into the alveoli, where its partial pressure is lower, and you breathe it out. The classic mistake is sending it through the pulmonary vein.
Second. Describe the pathway of blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations. Pause here to answer.

Start at the vena cava and name every structure in order, including the valves: right atrium, tricuspid, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, bicuspid, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, body, and back. Say where oxygen is gained and where it's lost. The classic mistake is saying the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-rich blood.

So, to trace oxygen, follow the air, then the blood, and check each gradient. Now picture both circuits as one loop, with a readout for how much oxygen it delivers every minute. Why can one body deliver so much more than another?
